Use this page every time you have pulled data into R and before you build
anything on it: it collects the commands for checking what an extract actually
contains. You need an extract to look at, so do [Phase 6 - First
extraction](first-extraction.qmd) first. When you are done you know the size,
column types, values, missing values and date ranges of your extract, and
whether each register you use reaches the end of your follow-up.

::: {.callout-note}
**`$` - access one column in a table** `data$koen` means: "the column `koen` in
the table `data`". Replace `data` with your own dataset name and `koen` with
your own column name. You will see `$` everywhere in R code.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**Want to practise the commands in RStudio?** All examples on the page use
`bef_data` - a BEF extract with columns such as `koen`, `alder` and `foed_dag`.
You can generate it with two lines, provided you have run the preparation block
in [Phase
6](first-extraction.qmd#preparation-install-fiktive-and-generate-synthetic-data):

```r
# Continuing from Phase 6 - bef_data is already opened as a lazy Arrow connection
bef_data <- bef_data %>% filter(year == 2015) %>% collect() # filter and fetch into R
```
:::

## The shape: size, columns and types {#the-shape}

```r
dim(bef_data) # number of rows and columns - e.g. "1200 rows, 8 columns"
nrow(bef_data) # number of rows only
ncol(bef_data) # number of columns only
names(bef_data) # column names as a vector
```

Those four work on data that is already in R. On a **lazy** object - one you have
opened but not yet `collect()`ed, called `bef` in the examples below - checking
the column names is fiddlier than it looks, and both of the obvious ways can
mislead you:

- `names()` on a lazy DuckDB connection made with `to_duckdb()` returns the
  *connection's* parts (`src`, `lazy_query`), not the table's columns.
- `colnames()` works on the DuckDB objects `read_register()` gives you, but on a
  lazy **Arrow** query that has been through `rename_with()` it can return
  `NULL` without any error, so columns that exist look missing. (Seen with
  arrow 23.0.1; other arrow versions may behave differently.)

The reliable version fetches the structure with zero rows:

```r
names(collect(head(bef, 0))) # column names of a lazy object, nothing read
```

`arrow::schema(bef)` also works on an Arrow connection and gives you the types
as well - see [`arrow::schema()`](function-guide.qmd#arrow-schema).

<details>
<summary>Example with simple data</summary>

```r
df <- data.frame(
  pnr        = c("001", "002", "003"),
  sex        = c("M", "F", "M"),
  index_date = as.Date(c("2015-03-01", "2016-07-14", "2014-11-30"))
)

names(df)
# [1] "pnr"        "sex"        "index_date"
```

</details>

**What type is each column?**

```r
glimpse(bef_data) # column name, type and first values - compact and readable (requires dplyr)
str(bef_data) # same information, but more verbose output
class(bef_data) # object type - is data actually in R, or is it still a connection?
class(bef_data$alder) # type for one column: "numeric", "character", "Date" etc.
```

`class(bef_data)` tells you whether you have real data
(`"data.frame"`/`"tbl_df"`) or still just an unsent query. You can see four
different kinds of return value:

- `"data.frame"` / `"tbl_df"` *without* `"prudent_duckplyr_df"` - data is in R. You can use all functions.
- `"prudent_duckplyr_df"` (followed by `"duckplyr_df" "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame"`) -
  a lazy DuckDB table from `read_parquet_duckdb()`, or from `read_register()` in fastreg 0.14.3 or newer. It says `"data.frame"`, but nothing is fetched yet. Missing `collect()`.
- `"FileSystemDataset"` (from `open_dataset()`) or `"tbl_duckdb_connection"` (from `to_duckdb()`, or from `read_register()` in fastreg 0.14.2 or older) -
  a lazy Arrow/DuckDB connection. Missing `collect()`.
- `"arrow_dplyr_query"` - an Arrow query with one or more piped steps (e.g.
  `filter()` or `select()`), but not yet executed. Missing `collect()`.

::: {.callout-tip}
**`class()` can help you debug** Does the object look like data but behave
strangely, or does your code fail with a mysterious message? Run
`class(your_object)` - if it is not `"data.frame"`, or it still includes
`"prudent_duckplyr_df"`, you are probably missing a `collect()`. The full table of what `class()` can return - and why - is in
[Phase 5 - Extracting data step by
step](extraction-step-by-step.qmd#check-do-you-have-data-or-just-a-connection).
:::

**What does a row actually look like?**

```r
head(bef_data) # the first 6 rows - do the columns and types look right?
head(bef_data, 10) # the first 10 rows
tail(bef_data) # the last 6 rows - useful for detecting incomplete datasets
```

## The values: what is actually in each column {#the-values}

::: {.callout-important}
**Two things must be in place before the commands in the rest of this section
work**

**1. Give your extraction a name.** If you just write `open_dataset(...)` or
`read_register(...)` without storing it in an object, R only prints a
quick preview and throws the result away - there is nothing to inspect
afterwards. Assign it a name with `<-` (see [Phase 2 - What is an
object?](r-intro.qmd#what-is-an-object)) so you can reuse it.

**2. Pull the data into R with `collect()` first.** Every command that uses `$`
(e.g. `table(bef$koen)`, `unique()`, `summary()`, `min()/max()/median()`,
`hist()`, `colSums(is.na())`) needs real data in R - `$` cannot extract a column
from a lazy Arrow/DuckDB connection. Check with `class(bef)`: if it does not say
`"data.frame"`/`"tbl_df"`, or it still says `"prudent_duckplyr_df"`, you are missing a `collect()`.

You do **not** rewrite `read_register()`/`open_dataset()` to pull the data in -
keep working with the object you already made. Reuse the name and store the
result, usually under the same name, so `bef` is overwritten and is now real
data. On a real register, always reduce it with `filter()`/`select()`
first:

```r
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(dplyr) # %>%, filter(), select(), collect()

bef <- read_register("bef") %>% # lazy connection - just a name so far
  rename_with(tolower) # column names to lower case

# reduce first, then fetch - overwrites bef (never collect() a whole register):
bef <- bef %>% filter(year == 2015) %>% select(pnr, koen, alder) %>% collect()

# now bef$koen, table(bef$koen), summary(bef) etc. all work
```

(If you want to keep the lazy connection, give the fetched data a new name
instead: `bef_2015 <- bef %>% filter(year == 2015) %>% collect()`.)

`glimpse()`, `head()` and dplyr verbs (`count()`, `filter()`,
`select()`) do work fine on the lazy connection, though (for column names, use
the zero-row trick above). So peek lazily,
`filter()`/`select()` it down, and `collect()` a small slice before you dig into
the values.
:::

As noted at the top of the page, `$` is R's way of saying "this column in this
table": `data$koen` is the column `koen` in the table `data`.

```r
unique(bef_data$koen) # which unique values exist in the koen column?
table(bef_data$koen) # frequency table: how many rows have each value?
table(bef_data$koen, bef_data$civst) # cross-table: distribution of sex across marital status
table(bef_data$koen, useNA = "ifany") # count NAs too - otherwise they are hidden (see warning below)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**`table()` hides NA by default.** Without `useNA = "ifany"`, `table()` only
counts the "real" values and drops missing values entirely - so the distribution
looks complete even when part of the column is `NA`. Always add
`useNA = "ifany"` (show the NA row only if NAs exist) or `useNA = "always"`
(always show the NA row) when inspecting a column, so you spot missing values
instead of overlooking them.
:::

<details>
<summary>Example with simple data</summary>

```r
# A small example with five patients and two variables:
df <- data.frame(
  sex          = c("M", "F", "M", "F", "M"),
  age_group    = c("18-40", "18-40", "41-60", "41-60", "41-60")
)

table(df$sex)
#  F  M
#  2  3       # 2 women, 3 men

table(df$sex, df$age_group)
#    18-40  41-60
# F      1      1    # 1 woman in 18-40, 1 woman in 41-60
# M      1      2    # 1 man in 18-40, 2 men in 41-60
```

</details>

## Summarise data

::: {.callout-note}
**What is NA?** `NA` (*Not Available*) is R's term for a missing or unknown
value. A cell can have `NA` because the information was not recorded, not
reported, or does not exist for that person. Most calculation functions return
`NA` if there is one `NA` in the data - unless you write `na.rm = TRUE` ("remove
NAs"). `is.na(x)` returns `TRUE` for NA values and `FALSE` for everything else.
:::

**When is NA a problem?** It depends on *which* column is missing:

- **NA in a key variable** (index date, pnr, outcome) is serious - these persons
  cannot be correctly included in the analysis, and you must decide whether to
  exclude them.
- **NA in a covariate** (e.g. income) can often be handled - e.g. with a
  separate "unknown" category or
  imputation ([Austin et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cjca.2020.11.010)).
- **NA from a join** means the person was not found in the right-hand dataset.
  What that means depends on the register. In an event register (prescriptions,
  hospital contacts) no row usually means no event, so `NA` is effectively a
  "no". In a status register (education, income, employment) no row means the
  information is unknown for that person, so `NA` is genuinely missing and
  must not be recoded to "none". Check what a missing row means for each
  register in your own delivery's documentation (DST's variable descriptions).

Always check `colSums(is.na(data))` immediately after an extraction or a join,
so you detect unexpected gaps before they propagate silently through the
analysis.

```r
summary(bef_data) # min, max, median, mean and quartiles for all columns
summary(bef_data$foed_dag) # summary of one column
```

For continuous variables:

```r
min(bef_data$alder, na.rm = TRUE) # smallest value (na.rm removes NAs - rm = remove)
max(bef_data$alder, na.rm = TRUE) # largest value
mean(bef_data$alder, na.rm = TRUE) # mean
median(bef_data$alder, na.rm = TRUE) # median
sd(bef_data$alder, na.rm = TRUE) # standard deviation
IQR(bef_data$alder, na.rm = TRUE) # interquartile range (Q3 - Q1)
```

## Check missing values

```r
sum(is.na(bef_data$koen)) # number of NAs in the koen column - replace with your own column name
colSums(is.na(bef_data)) # number of NAs per column - gives an overview of the entire dataset
```

`colSums(is.na(bef_data))` returns one line with a counter per column:

```
#  pnr  koen  alder  foed_dag  year  civst  opr_land  reg
#    0     0      0         3     0      0         0    0
```

Here `foed_dag` is missing for 3 - everything else is complete. A column with
`0` has no NAs at all.

::: {.callout-warning}
**`colSums(is.na())` counts only *true* `NA`.** In register data, "missing" is
often stored as an **empty or blank string** (whitespace) or a sentinel code -
not as `NA`. A column can therefore show `0` NAs and *still* be full of empty
values: e.g. a fixed-width key field filled with blanks (a 13-character field
that *looks* empty but is 13 spaces, not `NA`). So also check for blank values -
e.g. `sum(trimws(bef_data$pnr) == "", na.rm = TRUE)` - and look at
`nchar()`/`unique()` on a slice. This matters most for **join keys**: a
blank-but-not-`NA` key causes silent join errors (rows that look filled but
don't match).
:::

## Check dates

Date columns can contain impossible values - dates far outside the study period
are a sign of a conversion error or wrong column.

```r
min(bef_data$foed_dag, na.rm = TRUE) # is the earliest birth date plausible?
max(bef_data$foed_dag, na.rm = TRUE) # is the latest birth date plausible?

# Check for dates BEFORE an expected interval:
sum(bef_data$foed_dag < as.Date("1900-01-01"), na.rm = TRUE) # replace the date with your lower bound

# Check for dates AFTER an expected interval:
sum(bef_data$foed_dag > as.Date("2015-12-31"), na.rm = TRUE) # replace the date with your upper bound
```

See [DST
pitfalls](dst-pitfalls.qmd#4-date-columns-are-not-always-in-date-format) for the
most common date conversion errors and how to fix them.

## Check that every register reaches the end of your follow-up {#check-coverage}

A register in your delivery does not necessarily run as far as DST says the
register does. It may have been converted a year ago, ordered for fewer years,
or be a register that has closed for good (`dodsaars` stops in 2001, see
[pitfall 1](dst-pitfalls.qmd#death-registers)). Nothing errors when your
follow-up runs past the end of the data: people simply look as if nothing
happened to them, which quietly skews censoring, outcomes and matching.

So for **every** register you use, check its first and last year or date
against your study period before you build anything on it:

```r
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(dplyr) # summarise, collect

# Yearly registers (BEF, AKM, UDDA, FAIK ...): look at the year column
read_register("akm") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  summarise(first_year = min(year), last_year = max(year)) %>%
  collect()

# Event registers (LMDB, LPR, DOD ...): look at the event date itself
read_register("lmdb") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  summarise(first_date = min(eksd, na.rm = TRUE), last_date = max(eksd, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  collect()
```

For event registers, use the date column rather than `year`: `year` is the
[folder the row was filed under](dst-pitfalls.qmd#year-is-not-a-date), not
when the event happened.

The first and last date show only the two ends. One wrong date far in the
future is enough to make a register look complete, so count the rows per year
as well: a register that stops early has a last year with far fewer rows than
the years before it.

```r
# Rows per year of the event date: look for a year that is missing or much smaller
read_register("lmdb") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  count(eksd) %>% # rows per date, counted in DuckDB: one row per day comes back
  collect() %>%
  mutate(event_year = as.integer(format(eksd, "%Y"))) %>% # the year the event happened, now in R
  count(event_year, wt = n) %>% # add up the daily counts per year
  arrange(event_year) # oldest year first
```

The year is taken in R, after `collect()`, because the DuckDB backend that
newer fastreg versions use cannot translate `year()` and stops with an error
on a large register.

It also helps to know when the parquet copy was made. If the folder has not
changed in a long time, newer years are probably missing:

```r
file.info("path/to/parquet-registers/bef/")$mtime # replace with your project's path
```

If a register stops before your follow-up ends, either end follow-up at the
register's last date, or ask your data manager whether a newer delivery or the
raw SAS files cover the missing years.

Coverage is one of several things a delivery can get wrong. The rest are on
[Check your delivery](delivery-check.qmd).

<details>
<summary>More exploration: count, sort and quick plots</summary>

**Count and sort** (dplyr):

Replace `bef_data` with your own dataset name and column names with your own.

```r
bef_data %>% count(koen)               # number of rows per category
bef_data %>% count(koen, civst)        # per combination of two variables
bef_data %>% arrange(foed_dag)         # sort ascending by birth date
bef_data %>% arrange(desc(foed_dag))   # sort descending
```

**Quick visualisations** - for getting an overview, not for publication:

Replace `bef_data` with your own dataset name and column names with your own.

```r
# Continuous variables:
hist(bef_data$alder)                            # histogram
boxplot(bef_data$alder)                         # box plot
boxplot(alder ~ koen, data = bef_data)          # box plot split by sex

# Categorical variables:
barplot(table(bef_data$koen))                   # bar chart
```

</details>
